adults.title: Taste, Then Share
adults.big_idea: Gospel truths become sweet to us as we live them, and our joy grows when we love, share and invite so that others can partake too.
adults.objective: Learners will name one gospel truth that has become sweet to them through living it and choose one person to love, share with or invite this week.
prepare: Read Elder Stevenson's talk and 1 Nephi 8:10–12. Note that he spoke partly to Primary children; the truths are for everyone.
Write on the board: 1. Children of a loving Heavenly Father. 2. The great plan of happiness through Jesus Christ. 3. The gift of the Holy Ghost.
Bring a slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Ask learners to open the talk in Gospel Library, or bring three printed copies for the small groups.
Be aware that someone in the room may be grieving. Teach the story of the grieving priest gently.

segments.name: Looking or tasting
steps: Invite an opening prayer, then ask everyone to picture their favorite fruit. Ask one or two to describe it to the class.
Ask: How is hearing a fruit described different from tasting it yourself?
Explain that Elder Stevenson addressed part of his message to Primary children and used fruit to teach a truth for all of us. Read the first key quote (T34.07).
Let two or three people answer the question below. Keep it brief; this sets the theme for the whole lesson.
questions: When did a gospel truth stop being something you knew about and become something you had tasted?

segments.name: Lehi at the tree
steps: In pairs, read 1 Nephi 8:10–12. Ask pairs to look for two things: what the fruit did for Lehi, and the first thing he wanted afterward.

Hear a few findings. Then explain what Elder Stevenson taught: the tree stands for the love of God, shown most of all in the birth, life and atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ. The fruit stands for blessings received through His Atonement, including ordinances, covenants, the truths of the restored gospel and, ultimately, eternal life.
Ask the question below and let learners talk to each other, not only to you.
questions: Why do you think Lehi's joy turned so quickly into a desire for his family?

segments.name: Three fruits
steps: Divide into three groups and assign each one of the fruits on the board. A small class can take one fruit per person or pair.

Group 1 reads the section on being children of a loving Heavenly Father (T34.08–10) with Romans 8:16. Group 2 reads the section on the great plan of happiness (T34.11–14) with Alma 40:11–12. Group 3 reads the section on the gift of the Holy Ghost (T34.16–17) with 2 Nephi 32:5.
Give groups five minutes to answer the two questions below.
Give each group one minute to report. Ask them to share an experience, not a summary.
questions: What did Elder Stevenson teach about this truth?
What does living this truth look like on an ordinary day, and how has living it made it sweet to you?

segments.name: One visit, one question, one truth
steps: Retell the story in your own words: when Elder Stevenson lived in Japan he became friends with a Buddhist temple priest, a happy man who became deeply sad after his wife died. Elder Stevenson and a friend visited him one night. He was reluctant to talk until Elder Stevenson asked whether he knew where his wife was. They then shared that in God's loving plan her spirit was received into the spirit world, a state of rest, happiness and peace. His countenance changed in that moment.
Read the key quote from T34.12 about the transformation they witnessed.
Ask the questions below. Draw out how simple the visit was: they went, they asked, they shared one truth.
questions: What did Elder Stevenson and his friend actually do that evening?
Who do you know who might be waiting for someone to visit and share one truth?

segments.name: Love, share, invite
steps: Read Elder Stevenson's invitation and his promise (T34.20). Point out that he said to do this with words and actions.
Read President Oaks's words from this conference (T27.18) and note that the prophet and Elder Stevenson ask the same thing of us.

Hand out the slips of paper. Give two quiet minutes to write three lines: one gospel fruit that is sweet to me; one person who would be blessed to partake; whether I will love, share or invite this week, and how.
As a check for understanding, ask one or two volunteers to say in a sentence how tasting a truth differs from knowing about it.

segments.name: Close
steps: Bear a brief testimony of Jesus Christ and of one fruit of His gospel that is sweet to you.
Tell the class you will begin next week by asking: Whom did you love, share with or invite, and what joy came of it?
Close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: Gospel truths are the same. We learn them at home, Primary, and through the scriptures. They become sweet to us as we live them, bringing us happiness and joy.
Having this knowledge makes us stronger. This knowledge also makes us kinder to others, knowing that everyone around us is our brother or sister.
We witnessed a miraculous transformation: peace for despair, joy for sadness, hope for ashes.
As you do so, I promise that you will not only feel joy and happiness that comes as you partake of fruit of the gospel but even greater joy as loved ones around you partake as well.

scriptures.use: Read in pairs. Look for what the fruit did for Lehi and the first thing he wanted afterward.
Group 1 reads it with the section on being children of God and discusses how the Spirit has borne this witness to them.
Group 2 reads it with the story of the grieving priest and notes the words that describe where the spirits of the righteous are received.
Group 3 reads it with the section on the gift of the Holy Ghost and shares a time the Holy Ghost showed them what to do.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: I call upon all to act on these truths and to share them with others that we may all draw closer to Jesus Christ, our Savior.

invitations.text: I invite you to do something that is as simple as gospel fruit is delicious: love, share, and invite.

takeaways: Gospel truths become sweet when I live them, not only when I learn them.
Because of Jesus Christ there is peace for despair and joy for sadness.
My joy grows when I love, share and invite so that others can partake.
act: Pick one of the three fruits and live it on purpose each day this week; write a line each night about what you noticed.
Visit or call one person who is grieving or alone. Listen first, then share one truth that brings you peace.
Tell a family member or friend, in a sentence or two, why one gospel truth is sweet to you.
Invite someone to something you already do: a meal after church, home evening, sacrament meeting or a visit to the grounds of the house of the Lord.
music: I Am a Child of God
adapt: At home: skip the groups. Let each person choose one of the three fruits and tell the family why it is sweet to them, then write the three lines together.
Large class: have pairs, not groups, study the three fruits, and take reports from only one pair per fruit.
Short on time: do Looking or tasting, read 1 Nephi 8:10–12, and go straight to Love, share, invite.

youth.title: Don't Just Look at the Fruit
youth.big_idea: We find out how sweet the gospel of Jesus Christ is by living it, and the joy gets bigger when we love, share and invite.
youth.objective: Youth will explain in their own words why living a gospel truth is different from knowing about it, and will choose one real person to love, share with or invite this week.
prepare: Read Elder Stevenson's talk. He spoke partly to Primary children; tell the youth so, and that the three truths he taught are for every age.
Write the three fruits on the board: child of a loving Heavenly Father; the great plan of happiness through Jesus Christ; the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Draw three empty columns on the board headed Love, Share, Invite.
Ask youth to have scriptures or phones ready with the talk open in Gospel Library.
The talk includes a man grieving the death of his wife. Tell it honestly and gently.

segments.name: Describe it without naming it
steps: Start right after the prayer. In pairs, each person has 30 seconds to describe a favorite fruit without naming it while the partner guesses.
Ask: Suppose your partner had never tasted that fruit. Would your description be enough? Why not?
Read the first key quote (T34.07). Say that today is about tasting, not just describing.

segments.name: Lehi's first bite
steps: Have everyone open 1 Nephi 8:10–12. Race to find three words or phrases that describe the fruit, and the first thing Lehi wanted after he tasted it. First to find all four stands.

Explain what Elder Stevenson taught: the tree stands for the love of God, shown most of all in Jesus Christ. The fruit stands for the blessings that come through His Atonement, including the truths of the restored gospel.
Ask the question below. Take honest answers, including the ones that are not polished.
questions: What is one gospel truth you have only looked at so far, and one you would say you have actually tasted?

segments.name: Three fruits, three pitches
steps: Make three teams and give each one fruit from the board. Team 1 uses T34.08–10 and Romans 8:16. Team 2 uses T34.13–14 and Alma 42:8. Team 3 uses T34.16–17 and 2 Nephi 32:5.
Teams have four minutes to prepare a 30-second pitch with three parts: one line from Elder Stevenson, one phrase from the scripture, and what living this truth looks like at school on a Tuesday.
Hear the three pitches. After each, the other teams name the most real thing they heard.
Add anything missed: Elder Stevenson called being a child of God our most important identity, and he listed the Holy Ghost's roles as to warn, to comfort and to testify.

segments.name: When I don't feel good enough
steps: Say that many people wonder at times if they will ever be good enough. Invite a youth to read the key quote from T34.14.

Briefly tell the story: in Japan, Elder Stevenson had a friend, a Buddhist temple priest, who was overcome with grief after his wife died. Elder Stevenson and a friend visited him and shared that in God's plan her spirit was in the spirit world, in a state of rest, happiness and peace. His countenance changed in that moment.
Ask the questions below. Allow silence; do not rush to fill it.
questions: What is the good news in that quote, in your own words?
The priest's sadness turned to hope when he heard one truth. Which truth of the plan of happiness gives you the most hope right now?

segments.name: Love, share, invite
steps: Read Elder Stevenson's invitation and promise (T34.20). Note that he said to do it with words and actions.

Give the class two minutes to fill the three columns on the board with things a teenager could really do this week. Push for specifics: sit with someone, send a verse that helped you, bring a friend to an activity.
Read Elder Caussé's words about a testimony (T03.22). Ask how that takes the pressure off sharing.
Each youth types into phone notes, or writes on paper: one name, and one thing from the board they will do for that person by a day they choose.
Check for understanding: ask two volunteers to finish this sentence aloud: Knowing about a gospel truth is different from living it because...

segments.name: Close
steps: Share one fruit of the gospel that is sweet to you and bear testimony of Jesus Christ, the strength of youth.
Tell them you will open next week by asking who did it and what happened, and that a small try counts.
Close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: But once we have tasted it, we know how much we like it. Gospel truths are the same.
This is your most important identity.

Even when we make mistakes and feel discouraged or wonder if we will ever be good enough, “there is good news—wonderful, hopeful news! Because God loves [us], He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who took upon Himself [our] sins so [we] can repent, be forgiven, and keep progressing.”
As you do so, I promise that you will not only feel joy and happiness that comes as you partake of fruit of the gospel but even greater joy as loved ones around you partake as well.

scriptures.use: Everyone searches for three descriptions of the fruit and the first thing Lehi wanted after tasting it.
Team 1 uses a phrase from it in their pitch about being a child of God.
Team 2 finds the name this verse gives to God's plan and uses it in their pitch.
Team 3 uses it to explain what the Holy Ghost will do for those who receive Him.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Caussé
aligned_quotes.text: It need not be long, eloquent, or dramatic—it only needs to be true.

invitations.text: I invite you to do something that is as simple as gospel fruit is delicious: love, share, and invite.

takeaways: I find out how sweet a gospel truth is by living it.
Being a child of God is my most important identity.
Jesus Christ is the strength of youth, and my joy grows when I share Him.
act: Love: do one unasked act of kindness for the person whose name you wrote down.
Share: send a friend or family member one verse or one line from this talk that helped you, with a sentence about why.
Invite: ask one person to come with you to something you are already going to, such as a youth activity, seminary or church.
Taste: choose one of the three fruits and live it on purpose for seven days; notice what changes.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: skip teams. Each person takes one fruit and gives the 30-second pitch alone.
Large class: make six teams, two per fruit, and hear one pitch per fruit.
Short on time: do the opening game, 1 Nephi 8:10–12, and Love, share, invite.

children.title: Three Sweet Fruits
children.big_idea: The gospel of Jesus Christ makes me happy, and I can share it.
children.objective: Children will name three gospel truths that make them happy and choose one person to share a paper fruit with this week.
prepare: Draw a large tree with bare branches on the board or on a big sheet of paper.
Cut out three large paper fruits. Label them: I am a child of God. Jesus Christ and the plan of happiness. The Holy Ghost. Bring tape.
Cut out one small paper fruit for each child, and bring crayons.
Bring a soft ball, a blanket and a picture of the Savior.
Use paper fruit and pictures only. Do not bring real fruit or any food.

segments.name: Pick a fruit
steps: After the prayer, have the children stand, reach up high and pretend to pick fruit from a tall tree, then bend low and set it in a basket. Do it three times.
Let each child name a favorite fruit. Point out that we can look at a fruit and smell it, but we know how good it is when we taste it.

Tell them that at general conference Elder Stevenson, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, spoke especially to Primary children. He said he loved fruit when he was a boy, and he told us about fruit that makes us happy.

segments.name: Lehi's tree
steps: Point to the tree you drew. Tell the story from 1 Nephi 8:10–12 in simple words: the prophet Lehi saw a beautiful tree. He ate its fruit. It was sweeter than anything he had ever tasted, and it filled him with joy. Then he wanted his family to have some too.
Act it out together: walk in place to the tree, reach up, pretend to taste, put hands on hearts for joy, then wave for the family to come.
Explain that the tree reminds us of the love of God and of Jesus Christ. The fruit is like the blessings and truths of the gospel.
Teach the one truth with actions and repeat it three times: The gospel makes me happy (hands on heart), and I can share it (hands out).
questions: How do you think Lehi felt when he tasted the fruit?
Why did he call his family to come?

segments.name: Fruit one: I am a child of God
steps: Let a child tape the first paper fruit on the tree. Say: Heavenly Father knows you and loves you. You are His child.

Tell the story: Elder Stevenson was at a meeting with people who were having a very hard time. He asked the Primary children to stand and everyone to sing I Am a Child of God. A very young boy ran right up to the front, and Elder Stevenson picked him up. The boy sang every word in his sweet, loud voice, and the Spirit comforted the people.
Stand and sing I Am a Child of God the way that boy did.
Read Elder Fale's words from this conference (T14.01) and have the children say them with you.
questions: How do you feel when you sing that you are a child of God?

segments.name: Fruit two: Jesus Christ and the plan of happiness
steps: Let a child tape the second fruit on the tree. Hold up the picture of the Savior.
Say: Heavenly Father has a plan to help us be happy. It is called the great plan of happiness. Jesus Christ is at the center of it. When we make mistakes, Jesus helps us try again.
Sit in a circle and roll the ball. The child who catches it says: Jesus loves me, and names one thing they know about Jesus or one way He helps them. Roll until everyone has had a turn.
Tell them Elder Stevenson loves hearing Primary children sing about Jesus. If your children know Gethsemane, sing it together.

segments.name: Fruit three: the Holy Ghost
steps: Let a child tape the third fruit on the tree. Ask everyone to be very still. Whisper from across the room: Heavenly Father loves you. Ask what they needed to do to hear it.
Say: Elder Stevenson taught that the Holy Ghost warns, comforts and testifies. After we are baptized, we receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.
Wrap the blanket around a helper's shoulders, then let each child feel it. Say: The Holy Ghost comforts us, like a warm blanket.
Sing I Know My Father Lives. Ask them to listen for what the Spirit whispers.

segments.name: A fruit to share
steps: Read Elder Stevenson's invitation (T34.20). Say the three words together with actions: love (hug yourself), share (hands out), invite (wave someone over).
Give each child a small paper fruit and crayons. Ask them to color it and draw on it one of the three truths: themselves as a child of God, Jesus, or a quiet heart for the Holy Ghost.
While they draw, ask each child whom they will give it to: anyone they love, at home or anywhere else.
Check understanding: point to each fruit on the tree and let the children tell you what it is.
Tell them Elder Stevenson's promise in simple words: when we share the gospel with people we love, we feel even more joy.

segments.name: Say it and close
steps: Stand and say the truth with actions one more time: The gospel makes me happy, and I can share it.
Bear a short testimony that Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ know and love each child.
Tell them that next week you will ask who received their paper fruit and what they said when they gave it. Close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: You are some of the most valued and faithful members of the whole Church.
We are His children. Heavenly Father knows us personally.
They become sweet to us as we live them, bringing us happiness and joy.
As you do so, I promise that you will not only feel joy and happiness that comes as you partake of fruit of the gospel but even greater joy as loved ones around you partake as well.

scriptures.use: Tell it as a story in simple words while the children act it out; an older child may read verse 12 aloud.
Before singing I Am a Child of God, an older child reads it aloud; ask what the Spirit tells us about who we are.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

invitations.text: I invite you to do something that is as simple as gospel fruit is delicious: love, share, and invite.

takeaways: I am a child of God, and He loves me.
Jesus Christ helps me be happy.
I can share the gospel by loving, sharing and inviting.
act: Give your paper fruit to someone you love and tell them what you drew.
Sing I Am a Child of God for someone this week.
Do one kind thing for someone without being asked.
Invite someone to sing, pray or read a scripture story with you.
music: I Am a Child of God

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: keep the story to four sentences and act it out twice. Use helpers to tape the fruit and hold the blanket. Repeat the one truth with actions after every fruit, sing more and talk less, and let them simply color the paper fruit while you write the name of the person they choose.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: have a child read 1 Nephi 8:12 and Romans 8:16 aloud and another lead the ball activity. Ask a harder question: How is living a gospel truth like tasting a fruit, not just looking at it? Have them write on the back of the paper fruit one sentence about why that truth makes them happy.
